# English {#sec-english}

English translations of the prayer begin around AD 650 with a Northumbrian
version, and there have been many since. Three are in current liturgical use,
and all three are given here. All are based on Matthew rather than Luke.

## Book of Common Prayer, 1662

The version that shaped English prose, still used by the Church of England.

::: {.prayer lang="en" speech="en-GB" #en-bcp}
| Our Father, which art in heaven,
| Hallowed be thy Name;
| Thy kingdom come;
| Thy will be done
| in earth, as it is in heaven:
| Give us this day our daily bread;
| And forgive us our trespasses,
| as we forgive them that trespass against us;
| And lead us not into temptation,
| But deliver us from evil;
| For thine is the kingdom,
| the power, and the glory,
| For ever and ever.
| Amen.
:::

Note *which art*, not *who art*, and *in earth*, not *on earth* — both are
1662 readings that the traditional version below quietly modernised.

## Traditional ecumenical version

The lightly modernised form used across Catholic and many Protestant churches.

::: {.prayer lang="en" speech="en-GB" #en-traditional .variant}
| Our Father, who art in heaven,
| hallowed be thy name;
| thy kingdom come,
| thy will be done
| on earth as it is in heaven.
| Give us this day our daily bread,
| and forgive us our trespasses,
| as we forgive those who trespass against us;
| and lead us not into temptation,
| but deliver us from evil.
:::

Most Protestants close with the doxology: *For thine is the kingdom, the power,
and the glory, for ever and ever. Amen.* At Mass in the Catholic Church the
embolism is followed instead by: *For the kingdom, the power and the glory are
yours, now and for ever.*

## English Language Liturgical Consultation, 1988

The modern ecumenical translation, and the one that departs furthest from the
familiar wording.

::: {.prayer lang="en" speech="en-GB" #en-ellc .variant}
| Our Father in heaven,
| hallowed be your name,
| your kingdom come,
| your will be done,
| on earth as in heaven.
| Give us today our daily bread.
| Forgive us our sins
| as we forgive those who sin against us.
| Save us from the time of trial
| and deliver us from evil.
| For the kingdom, the power, and the glory are yours
| now and for ever. Amen.
:::

*Save us from the time of trial* is the ELLC's answer to the sixth petition,
avoiding the implication that God does the leading. *Sins* replaces
*trespasses*, moving back toward the Greek *ὀφειλήματα*.

## On the doxology

*For thine is the kingdom, the power, and the glory* is not in the oldest
manuscripts and is not considered part of Matthew's text. The translators of
the 1611 King James Bible believed the Greek manuscript they had was ancient
and took it in; its use in English dates from at least the 1549 First Prayer
Book of Edward VI, influenced by Tyndale's 1526 New Testament. The Latin
liturgical tradition never attached it to the prayer at all.
